title: Cc No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju vs . Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 Of 31 on 4 March, 2017
full_text: Cc No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju vs . Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 Of 31 on 4 March, 2017 IN THE COURT OF METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE (T) NORTH­EAST, KARKARDOOMA COURTS, DELHI Presiding Officer: Dinesh Kumar, DJS CC No. 48331/2015 In the matter of: Smt. Manju, W/o Sh. Ashok Kumar R/o H.No. 895, Gali No.25, 4 ½ Pusta, Sonia Vihar, Delhi­110094. .........Complainant. Vs Sh. Devender Kumar Pandey s/o Sh. Salik Ram Pandey R/o H. No.B­73, Gali No.3, North Ghonda, Delhi­110053. ..........Accused. JUDGMENT Date of Institution of complaint :26.02.2014 Offence Complained of : Section 138 , NI Act Date of Reserving the Judgment :28.02.2017 Date of Decision :04.03.2017 Plea of accused :Not Guilty Final Order :Acquitted Present:­ Sh. Sanjeev Shukla, learned counsel for complainant. Sh. Balvinder Singh, learned counsel for accused. CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 BRIEF REASONS FOR THE ORDER 1. The present complaint has been filed under Section 138 , Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter called the NI Act ). The case of the complainant is as under:­ 1.1. Subhash, brother­in­law of the complainant, had introduced Smt. Manju, the complainant herein with Devender Kumar Pandey, the accused herein. The complainant wanted to purchase a property. The accused told the complainant that he was going to sell one of his properties. The complainant became ready to purchase the property of the accused for a total consideration of Rs. 9,60,000/­. The complainant paid the earnest money of Rs. 1,60,000/­ to the accused before her brother in law namely Subhash on 06.08.2013. It was agreed that the balance amount of Rs. 8,00,000/­ would be paid by the complainant on or before 06.11.2013. 1.2. On 30.10.2013 the complainant paid the balance amount of Rs. 8,00,000/­ to the accused. However, when the complainant asked for execution of registry of the property, the accused delayed the matter under one pretext or the other. Late on, the complainant came to know that accused was not the owner of the said property. 1.3. The complainant demanded back her abovesaid amount CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 of Rs. 9,60,000/­ from the accused. The accused, in order to discharge the above said liability, had issued four cheques. The accused had assured that the cheques would be honoured on presentation. 1.4. Out of these four cheques, the complainant presented two cheques bearing No. 583657 dated 14.12.2013 for Rs. 1,00,000/­ and cheque bearing no. 583658 dated 18/12/2013 for Rs. 1,00,000/­, both drawn on Bank of Baroda, Bhajanpura, Delhi with her banker i.e. Indian Bank, Main Road, 1 st Pusta, Sonia Vihar, Delhi for encashment. However, both the cheques were returned unpaid with the remarks 'Funds Insufficient" vide return memo dated 24/01/2014. 1.5. A legal notice dated 06/02/2014 was sent to the accused by the complainant through his counsel through registered post. The service of the legal notice was duly effected, however, the accused did not receive the legal notice as the registered envelope was returned to the counsel for the complainant. The accused failed to make the payment. Hence, the present complaint has been filed. 2. The Court examined the complainant on oath. After perusing the material available on record, the Court took the cognizance and process was issued against the accused. Accused appeared in the Court. He was released on bail. 3. The notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C. was served upon CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 the accused. He pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. As per the judgment of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in matter titled Rajesh Aggarwal Vs. State & Anr , Crl. M.C. no. 1996/2010 & Crl. M.A. no. 7672/2010, decided on 12.07.2010, his plea of defence was recorded. The accused would state that the complainant had paid Rs. 6,60,000/­ to him. She could not pay the balance amount. He had returned Rs. 4,60,000/­ in cash to the complainant and only Rs. 2,00,000/­ were remained to be paid. There was no such liability as claimed by the complainant. He had issued two cheques to the complainant as security to make the balance payment. However, after some time, the complainant called him and told that she had lost those cheques during shifting of her house. The complainant demanded other cheques. He had given two other cheques thereafter. The cheques were security cheques. He had not received the legal notice. 4. The opportunity was granted to the accused to cross examine the witnesses of complainant. The complainant examined herself as CW­1 to prove her case. She has tendered her evidence by way of affidavit and reiterated the facts stated in the complaint. She has relied upon the following documents: a)Original cheque bearing no. 583657 dated 14/12/2013 for Rs. 1,00,000/­, drawn on Bank of Baroda, Bhajanpura, Delhi is Ex. CW1/A. b)Original cheque bearing no. 583658 dated CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 18/12/2013 for Rs. 1,00,000/­, drawn on Bank of Baroda, Bhajanpura, Delhi is Ex. CW1/B. c) Cheque return memo dt. 24/01/2014 are Ex. CW1/C & Ex. CW1/D. d)Copy of legal notice dated 06/02/2014 is Ex. CW1/E. e) Postal receipt is Ex. CW 1/F f) The returned envelope along with returned AD card is Ex. CW1/G. 5. The complainant also examined Sh. Subhash Chand, brother­in law of the complainant, as CW2, and her husband Sh. Ashok Kumar as CW3. Both the witnesses had deposed, inter alia, that complainant had paid Rs. 9,60,000/­ to the accused to purchase his property. However, later on, it was discovered that accused was not the owner of the property. He failed to return the money. Witness CW3 has further stated that accused had issued cheques in question to his wife which were dishonoured on presentation. 6. All the witnesses were cross examined and thereafter, CE was closed. 7. The accused was examined and his statement was recorded under Section 313 Cr.P.C. by putting all the incriminating evidence to him on 17/05/2016. The accused had reiterated his defence disclosed at the time of receiving notice under Section 251 Cr.P.C. in the Court. He had admitted that CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 complainant had agreed to purchase the property for a sum of Rs. 9,60,000/­. The complainant had paid only Rs. 6,60,000/­ to the accused, therefore, he did not execute the documents of the property in favour of the complainant. He was the owner of the said property. He had issued two cheques to the complainant. Later on, the complainant had stated that she had misplaced those cheques. Therefore, he had issued fresh two cheques to the complainant. He would further state that he had already made the payment of Rs. 4,60,000/­ to the complainant before issuance of cheques in question. He was not liable to pay amount as claimed by the complainant. The accused had also stated that he did not receive any legal notice under Section 138 NI Act. 8. The accused led defence evidence and examined himself as DW1. He has deposed that in July 2013, the complainant had approached him to purchase his property for a total sum of Rs. 9,60,000/­. The complainant paid earnest money of Rs. 1,60,000/­ in cash on 06.08.2016 (sic). The balance payment of Rs. 8,00,000/­ was to be made on or before 30.10.2013. The complainant could pay only Rs. 6,60,000/­ till 30.10.2016 (sic) including the earnest money. As the complainant had failed to make the entire payment, the deal was cancelled. The accused agreed to return the amount. He paid Rs. 4,60,000/­ to the complainant on 22.11.2013 and promised to pay the balance amount of Rs. 2,00,000/­ by mid CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 December 2013. The complainant approached him in first week of December 2013. The accused did not have cash at that time. Therefore, he had issued two cheques bearing No. 583657 and 583658 as security. He had asked the complainant not to present the cheques and to return them after receiving the amount. The complainant contacted him in January 2014 and told that she had lost the cheques, therefore he issued fresh two cheques bearing No. 522839 and 522840 as security. On 26.03.2014, he made the remaining payment and demanded his cheques back. The complainant promised to return the cheques. He believed the complainant. When he received the summons of the court, he came to know that complainant had misused his cheques. The witness has further deposed that the complainant got issued the legal notice on a wrong address despite knowing his correct address. Therefore, the accused did not receive the legal notice. Had he received the legal notice, he would have replied the same. 9. The witness was cross examined. Accused did not examine any other witness. Therefore DE was closed and matter was fixed for final arguments. However, at that stage, the complainant moved an application U/s 311 Cr. P.C for re­ examining the complainant to bring on record certain documents stated to be executed by the accused in his favour. The said application was allowed vide order dated 21.11.2016. The complainant was re­examined. She relied upon the CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 following documents: a) Agreement between complainant and accused is Ex.CW1/R1. b) Agreement to Sell, GPA, Will, Receipt, Possession letter and undertaking are Ex. CW1/R2 (colly 15 pages). 10. The witness was cross examined. Thereafter, supplementary statement of the accused u/s 313 Cr. P.C was recorded. The accused admitted that the documents were executed. However, the deal was not finalized and therefore documents did not have any relevance. He had not given the documents to the complainant. He does not know how the complainant came in possession of those documents. 11. The accused re­examined himself as DW1. In his re­ examination as DW1 he has deposed that he had not given those documents to the complainant. He does not know how the complainant came in possession of those documents. He had already sold the said property in the year 2013. 12. The witness was cross examined. The DE was closed and the matter was fixed for final arguments. 13. Ld. Counsel for the complainant would argue that the complainant has proved her case beyond reasonable doubts and therefore, the guilt of the accused has been proved as per law. Complainant has proved the cheques, returning memo, legal notice and postal receipts. The accused had issued the impugned CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 cheques to discharge his legal liability. Accused has taken a false defence. The accused has failed to discharge the initial burden. He has failed to prove that he had repaid the amount as alleged. There are sufficient documents on court record to prove that accused had taken a total sum of Rs. 9,60,000/­ from the complainant. However, he did not transfer the property in the name of the complainant. Hence, it is proved that accused was liable to make the payment, however, he did not make the payment within stipulated time. It is also proved that all the steps were taken by the complainant within the time provided by the law. The defence taken by the accused is false and concocted. Therefore, the case of the complainant is proved as per law. Hence, the accused may be convicted for the offence under Section 138 , NI Act. 14. Per contra, Ld. counsel for the accused would argue that the complainant has failed to prove her case against the accused beyond reasonable doubts. The complainant had paid a total sum of Rs. 6,60,000/­ only to the accused. She has failed to pay the balance amount. Therefore, he did not transfer the property in the name of the complainant. However, he had repaid amount of Rs. 4,60,000/­ to the complainant immediately. He had issued two cheques to the complainant as security for payment of balance amount of Rs. 2,00,000/­. At her request, he had given two fresh cheques again. Later on, he had paid the entire amount. However, the complainant has CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 misused the cheques in question. Further the complainant issued the notice at wrong address despite knowing the correct address of the accused. Therefore, accused had not received the legal notice. Hence, the complaint is not maintainable. There are various contradictions in the testimonies of CW2 and CW3. The witnesses in their statements have stated that accused had shown forged documents. However, in their cross examination witness stated that no documents were shown. Further the witness has stated that when complainant went to take possession of property, it was disclosed that person residing therein was owner and he did not allow the complainant to enter the property. However, in his cross examination witness CW2 has stated that no inquiry was made from the person residing in the property. Therefore, the testimonies of the witnesses are not reliable. They are family members of the complainant. They are not trustworthy. The complainant has misused the security cheques. Therefore, it is prayed, accused may be acquitted. 15. I have heard the rival submissions of the learned counsels of the parties and carefully perused the material on record. 16. In the present case, it is an admitted fact that accused and complainant are known to each other. It is also proved on record that the cheques bear the signatures of the accused and that they had been drawn on an account maintained by the CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 accused. It has been proved on Court record that the cheques were dishonored on presentation. It is also admitted by the accused that he himself had handed over the cheques in question to the complainant. 17. The defence of the accused, however, is that he had not issued the cheques to the complainant to discharge legal liability as alleged. He had given the cheques to the complainant as security. He had already repaid the entire amount. The complainant has misused the security cheques. Therefore, the question involved in the present case, inter alia, is whether the accused had any legal liability to make payment to the complainant and whether he had issued the cheques to the complainant to discharge his legal liability. Further the accused has also taken the defence that he had not received legal notice under Section 138 NI Act. Therefore, maintainability of the complaint is also to be decided in view of the said defence. 18. Section 138 of the Act provides that where a cheques is dishonoured, the person drawing the cheque shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provision of the Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque or with both. Chapter XVII comprising Sections 138 to 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act was introduced in the statute by Act 66 of 1988. The object underlying the provision contained in the said CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 Chapter was aimed at inculcating faith in the efficacy of banking operations and giving credibility to negotiable instruments in business and day to day transactions by making dishonour of such instruments an offence. The said provisions were intended to discourage people from not honouring their commitments by way of payment through cheques. One of the important aspect to be noted is that the law provides a rebuttable presumption in favour of the complainant and against the accused. Before discussing further, it would be useful to quote the language of the relevant provisions of the law as provided under the Negotiable Instrument Act . Sections 118 , Section 138 , and Section 139 of the Act are important Sections for the purpose of further discussion. These Sections read as under: "118. Presumptions as to negotiable instruments. ­ Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made: (a) of consideration: that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration; ... "138. Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account. ­ Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provision of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless­ (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier. (b)the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice, in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation. ­ For the purposes of this section, 'debt or other liability' means a legally enforceable debt or other liability. "139. Presumption in favour of holder.­ It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt, or other liability." 19. Perusal of law as discussed hereinabove would show that there is a presumption in favour of the complainant and against the accused. However, the presumption is rebuttable. An accused for discharging the burden of proof placed upon him under a statute need not examine himself. He may discharge his burden on the basis of the material already CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 brought on record. Standard of proof on the part of the accused and that of the prosecution in a criminal case is different. Whereas prosecution must prove the guilt of an accused beyond all reasonable doubt, the standard of proof so as to prove a defence on the part of the accused is 'preponderance of probabilities'. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which complainant relies. This has been so held in various judgments of the Apex Court of India. Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Rangappa vs Sri Mohan (2010) 11 SCC 441 had the occasion to discuss the law in detail on this aspect. After discussing the various case laws on this issue their Lordships have held as under: "13. With regard to the facts in the present case, we can also refer to the following observations in M.M.T.C. Ltd. and Anr. v. Medchl Chemicals & Pharma (P) Ltd. , (2002) 1 SCC 234 (Para. 19): "... The authority shows that even when the cheque is dishonoured by reason of stop payment instruction, by virtue of Section 139 the Court has to presume that the cheque was received by the holder for the discharge in whole or in part, of any debt or liability. Of course this is a rebuttable presumption. The accused can thus show that the `stop payment' instructions were not issued because of insufficiency or paucity of funds. If the accused shows that in his account there was sufficient funds to clear the amount of the cheque at the time of presentation of CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 the cheque for encashment at the drawer bank and that the stop payment notice had been issued because of other valid causes including that there was no existing debt or liability at the time of presentation of cheque for encashment, then offence under Section 138 would not be made out. The important thing is that the burden of so proving would be on the accused. ..." (emphasis supplied) 14. In light of these extracts, we are in agreement with the respondent­claimant that the presumption mandated by Section 139 of the Act does indeed include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. To that extent, the impugned observations in Krishna Janardhan Bhat (supra) may not be correct. However, this does not in any way cast doubt on the correctness of the decision in that case since it was based on the specific facts and circumstances therein. As noted in the citations, this is of course in the nature of a rebuttable presumption and it is open to the accused to raise a defence wherein the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability can be contested. However, there can be no doubt that there is an initial presumption which favours the complainant. Section 139 of the Act is an example of a reverse onus clause that has been included in furtherance of the legislative objective of improving the credibility of negotiable instruments. While Section 138 of the Act specifies a strong criminal remedy in relation to the dishonour of cheques, the rebuttable presumption under Section 139 is a device to prevent undue delay in the course of litigation. However, it must be remembered that the offence made punishable by Section 138 can be better described as a regulatory offence since the bouncing of a cheque is largely in the nature of a civil wrong whose impact is usually confined to the private parties involved in commercial CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 transactions. In such a scenario, the test of proportionality should guide the construction and interpretation of reverse onus clauses and the accused/defendant cannot be expected to discharge an unduly high standard or proof. In the absence of compelling justifications, reverse onus clauses usually impose an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. Keeping this in view, it is a settled position that when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of `preponderance of probabilities'. Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. As clarified in the citations, the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own." (Emphasis supplied) 20. Thus it has been settled that there is a presumption in favour of the complainant and against the accused, that the cheque was issued for consideration. However, the presumption is rebuttable. The accused can prove that the cheque was not issued for consideration and that the accused did not have any liability to pay the amount. It has also been held that the accused need not lead evidence in support of his defence. He can prove it on the balance of probabilities by showing the contradictions in the material produced by the complainant. 21. In the present case, the accused has admitted that he himself had handed over the cheques to the complainant. He has CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 stated that he had given the cheques as security. However, there is no evidence on court record to prove his contention. Mere self serving averment of the accused is not sufficient to prove this fact. 22. The complainant has examined herself as CW1 to prove her case. She has deposed that she had paid Rs. 9,60,000/­ in total to the accused to purchsae his property. However, the accused did not transfer the property in her name. Thereafter, he had issued the cheques in question to discharge his legal liability. 23. The witness has been cross examined. The accused has admitted that he had entered into an agreement to sell his property to the complainant for a sum of Rs. 9,60,000/­. Thus, the relationship between the parties is admitted. It has also been admitted by the accused in his evidence as DW1 that he had not transferred any property to the complainant. He has also admitted that he had sold the said property to someone else. Therefore, it is proved on the record that the accused was legally liable to return the money which he had received from the complainant for the abovesaid transaction of the property. 24. The case of the complainant is that she had paid Rs. 9,60,000/­ to the accused. On the other hand, the accused has stated that he had received only Rs. 6,60,000/­ from the complainant. However, it is note worthy that in his examination u/s 313 Cr. P.C on 08.12.2016, the accused has admitted that he CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 had executed the documents Ex. CW1/R1 and Ex. CW1/R2 (colly 15 pages). Further in his evidence as DW1 also, he had admitted execution of these documents. Thus, the documents Ex CW1/R1 and Ex. CW1/R2 (colly 15 pages) are proved as per law. 25. Perusal of Ex. CW1/R1 would show that complainant had paid Rs. 1,60,000/­ as earnest money to the accused. The accused also has admitted receiving of this amount. Further, page 11 of Ex. CW1/R1 (colly 15 pages) is a receipt shown to be executed by the accused. This receipt contains that Devender Kumar Pandey, accused herein, had received a sum of Rs. 9,60,000/­ in cash from Smt. Manju, the complainant herein. The accused has admitted the execution of this document. There is no explanation as to why he had executed the receipt of Rs. 9,60,000/­ if he had received only Rs. 6,60,000/­ from the complainant. He has failed to provide any plausible reason for execution of said document. He has failed to lead any evidence, except his self serving averment, to prove that he had received only Rs. 6,60,000/­ from the complainant. Thus, it has been proved on court record beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had received a sum of Rs. 9,60,000/­ in total from the complainant as consideration for transferring his property. It has been proved that the accused did not transfer the property in favour of the complainant. Therefore, he was legally liable to pay Rs. 9,60,000/­ to the complainant. CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 26. The accused has taken the defence that he had returned Rs. 6,60,000/­ to the complainant. However, there is no documentary evidence to prove this payment beyond reasonable doubts. As per law of evidence, the burden to prove a fact is on the party who asserts it. In the present case, it is the accused who has asserted that he had repaid Rs. 6,60,000/­ to the complainant. The complainant cannot be asked to bring negative evidence to prove that she had not received amount of Rs. 6,60,000/­ from the accused. No such evidence is possible. Therefore, it is the accused who must bring some positive evidence to prove this payment to the complainant. However, there is no such evidence on court record. In these circumstances, I hold that the accused has failed to prove that he had repaid the amount of Rs. 6,60,000/­ to the complainant. 27. In the light of discussion hereinabove, I hold that the complainant was entitled to recover Rs. 9,60,000/­ from the accused. The accused has failed to discharge the initial burden. Therefore, the complainant has proved beyond reasonable doubts that the accused had issued the cheques in question to the complainant to discharge his legal liability. It has been proved on record that the cheques were dishonoured on presentation. 28. The complainant as CW1 has deposed that after dishonouring of the cheques, she had issued a legal notice under Section 138 NI Act to the accused through registered post. In CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 her affidavit of evidence, she has further stated that accused did not receive the legal notice as registered envelope was returned to the counsel for the complainant. Thus, even as per the case of the complainant the accused had not received the legal notice under Section 138 NI Act. 29. Ld. counsel for the complainant would argue that the complainant had issued the legal notice under Section 138 NI Act at the address of the accused. However, the accused manipulated the report. Therefore, the notice was returned unserved. However, the presumption of service of legal notice is to be drawn as the legal notice was sent through post. Ld. Counsel has relied upon the postal receipt Ex. CW1/F and the returned envelope Ex. CW1/G. 30. I have considered the submissions. Perusal of the envelope Ex. CW1/G would show that this registered post envelope has been returned with the endorsement "3 mein is prakar ghar no. nahi hai." Thus, it has been shown that the accused had not received the legal notice under Section 138 NI Act. There is nothing on court record to prove that the accused had manipulated the report on the postal article. There is nothing on record to prove that accused had the knowledge of the legal notice. There is no presumption of service of legal notice under Section 138 NI Act. Service is to be proved by the complainant if it is disputed by the accused. I get strength from the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in HDFC Bank Ltd. CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 Vs. Amit Kumar Singh 2009 (4) Crimes 772 (Del.). In HDFC Bank Ltd. Vs. Amit Kumar Singh, Crl. Rev. P. No. 296/2009, decided on 22.05.2009, in the matter before the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi the question was whether the complainant was required to prove service of legal notice by leading evidence. In the said case, the Trial Court had dismissed the complaint of the complainant as the complainant had not filed any delivery report or AD Card or proof of delivery of the demand notice. Hon'ble High Court has upheld the order of Ld. MM. Learned Counsel for the petitioner had submitted before the Hon'ble High Court that the learned MM erred in not drawing the presumption under Section 27 of the GC Act. He referred to the observations of the Supreme Court in K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidya Balan as well as C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed . As long as the complaint contained the basic fact regarding the mode and manner of issuance of notice to the drawer of cheque, the court should hold that the requirement of Section 138 NI Act was satisfied and consequently cognizance should be taken of the offence. He referred to Sections 94 , 118 , 138 and 139 NI Act as well as Section 3 , 114 of the EA read with Section 27 of GC Act to contend that the presumption of service of notice should be drawn since the legal notice was sent by registered post to the drawer at the address of the drawer as available in the records of the complainant. It was contended before Hon'ble Court that since the legal notice was sent by CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 properly addressing the drawer at the address available in the records of the complainant, the complainant had discharged its part in terms of Section 138 (b) NI Act. Counsel for the petitioner also referred to Section 94 NI Act and submitted that once the notice was sent by post, it would amount to a notice of dishonor in terms of Section 138 NI Act as well. It is submitted that the learned MM urged in holding that Section 94 applies only in a situation where civil liability is sought to be enforced. Counsel also referred to Section 144 NI Act. 31. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in HDFC Bank Ltd. Vs. Amit Kumar Singh (supra) dismissed all these submissions with a detailed order. Hon'ble High Court first observed that proceedings under Section 138 , NI Act being criminal proceedings, Section 94 of the Act was not applicable. It has also been held that presumption of service of legal notice can not be taken in criminal proceedings. Hon'ble High Court has held as under: "15. There can be no doubt that Section 138 has been introduced into the NI Act as a penal provision. The NI Act was otherwise not a criminal law statute. Chapter XVII NI Act was introduced to make the dishonor of the cheque for insufficiency of funds a punishable offence. The object of the introduction of Chapter XVII was no doubt to have a deterrent effect on unscrupulous drawers of cheques who were issuing cheques thus without any intention of making payment. Sections 138 to 147 NI Act are criminal law provisions and have, therefore, to be strictly construed. At the outset, this Court therefore, CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 rejects the plea that the principles informing Section 94 NI Act regarding notice of dishonour of a cheque should be incorporated pro tanto into Sections 138 to 147 NI Act. "16. The above legal position is consistent with the legislative intent of the Parliament in enacting Section 144 NI Act. Although this provision talks of the mode of service of summons to either a witness or an accused under the NI Act , this Court finds no reason why the same standard should not be insisted upon for service of legal notice upon the accused by the complainant prior to the filing of the complaint. The reason for this is that whenever a summoning order is passed and summons are sent to the accused, it would be sent at the same address shown for the accused in the complaint. This address ought not to be any different from the address in the legal notice. It is therefore a continuous chain of events. First there is a dishonor of the cheque. Next is the legal notice to be sent to the drawer within 30 days of the payee receiving an intimation from the Bank of the dishonor of the cheque. Such legal notice in writing has to be addressed to the drawer at the address of the drawer available with the complainant such notice. Such notice has to be received by the drawer and he should fail to make payment within 15 days after receipt of such notice. This chain thereafter continues into the next stage following the failure to make the payment. The complainant or the drawee then approaches the criminal court with a complaint in which he will implead as the accused, the drawer of the cheque, with the address being shown as the same to which the legal notice was sent. The summon, therefore, goes to the same address. "17. In a situation where there is no proof of delivery submitted before the Court to show that the legal notice has in fact been received by the accused if a presumption is to be drawn and after taking cognizance summons are CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 issued to the accused at the same address, it would either not be received back at all or received back with the remarks that the accused is not available at the address. Thereafter no further progress can be made in the criminal complaint. This is an outcome that ought to be avoided. Therefore, the appropriate course to be adopted, which is also the more practical one, is to insist on the same standard of proof of service of the legal notice as that envisaged under Section 144 NI Act in the context of summons. "18. Section 144 NI Act reads as under :­ "144. Mode of service of summons.__(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure , 1973 (2 of 1974), and for the purposes of this Chapter, a Magistrate issuing a summons to an accused or a witness may direct a copy of summons to be served at the place where such accused or witness ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works; for gain, by speed post or by such courier services as are approved by a Court of Session. "(2) Where an acknowledgment purporting to be signed by the accused or the witness or an endorsement purported to be made by any person authorised by the postal department or the courier services that the accused or the witness refused to take delivery of summons has been received, the Court issuing the summons may declare that the summons has been duly served." 32. This will be minimum requirement in CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. It will be seen from the above provision that it is a hybrid of Sections 62 and 69 CrPC. Under Section 62 CrPC summons have to be served upon the accused personally. Section 144 NI Act in that sense carves out an exception to Section 62 CrPC since it permits service of summons to both the accused and the witness by registered post. Under Section 62 CrPC, the Courts have consistently held that summons to an accused cannot be sent by registered post but must be to be delivered personally. The relevant decisions in this regard are Guthikonda Sri Hari Prasada Rao v. Guthikonda Lakshmi Rajyma 1990 CriLJ 1594, S. Bhupinder Singh Makkar v. Narinder Kaur 1990 CriLJ 2265 and Meenaz Moloobhay v. State of Maharashtra 2000 CriLJ 3998. It is only under Section 69 CrPC that summons to a witness can be sent by registered post. The language of Sections 144 (2) and 69 (2) NI Act are identical. It is plain from Section 144(2) that summons to a person, who is arraigned as an accused in a complaint under Section 138 NI Act, when sent by registered A/D post has to be followed by placing before the Court either the signed acknowledgement due card purported to be signed by the addressee, or an endorsement by the postal department or the courier service that the accused refused to take delivery of the summons. In the absence of such acknowledgement or endorsement of the postal authority or the courier services, the Court will not draw a presumption that such summons have been duly served. In the concerned view of this Court therefore, the learned MM was in the instant case perfectly justified in insisting that the complainant should show to the CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. In such cases, it would be for the Court to draw an inference that service must be presumed. It was in that context that the Court had posed a question: whether there was difference between a notice which has been returned unclaimed or a notice that has been returned after having been refused by the accused? In that context, it was stated that the principle incorporated in Section 27 of the GC Act can "profitably be imported in such a case". It was held that in that situation the deeming provision of Section 27 of the GC Act would be attracted and it would be for the drawer (noticee) to prove that it was not really served and that he was not CC No. 48331/15 Smt. In the instant case, however, nothing has been heard by the complainant after sending the notice by registered post. The notice has not been returned unserved. No proof of delivery report has been filed. There is no postal endorsement or certificate by the courier service agency to the effect that the noticee refused service. "21. In D. Vinod Shivappa v. Nanda Belliappa (2006) 6 SCC 456 the Supreme Court discussed in detail the rationale behind the provision and envisaged three possible situations (SCC, p.462): "If a notice is issued and served upon the drawer of the cheque, no controversy arises. Similarly if the notice is refused by the addressee, it may be presumed to have been served. This is also not disputed. This leaves us with the third situation where the notice could not be served on the addressee for one or the other reason, such as his non­availability at the time of delivery, or premises remaining locked on account of his having gone elsewhere, etc. etc. If in each such case the law is understood to mean that there has been no service of notice, it would completely defeat the very purpose of the Act. It would then be very easy for an unscrupulous and dishonest drawer of a cheque to make himself scarce for some time after issuing the cheque so that the requisite statutory notice can never be served upon him and consequently he can never be prosecuted. There is good authority to support the proposition that once the complainant, the payee of the cheque, issues notice to the drawer of the cheque, the cause of action to file a complaint arises on the expiry of the period prescribed for payment by the drawer of the cheque. If he does not file a complaint within one month of the date on which the cause of CC No. 48331/15 Smt. Manju Vs. Devender Kumar Pandey Page 31 of 31 action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to Section 138 of the Act, his complaint gets barred by time. Thus, a person who can dodge the postman for about a month or two, or a person who can get a fake endorsement made regarding his non­ availability can successfully avoid his prosecution because the payee is bound to issue notice to him within a period of 30 days from the date of receipt of information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid. He is, therefore, bound to issue the legal notice which may be returned with an endorsement that the addressee is not available on the given address. "15. We cannot also lose sight of the fact that the drawer may by dubious means manage to get an incorrect endorsement made on the envelope that the premises has been found locked or that the addressee was not available at the time when postman went for delivery of the letter. It may be that the address is correct and even the addressee is available but a wrong endorsement is manipulated by the addressee. In such a case, if the facts are proved, it may amount to refusal of the notice. If the complainant is able to prove that the drawer of the cheque knew about the notice and deliberately evaded service and got a false endorsement made only to defeat the process of law, the court shall presume service of notice. This, however, is a matter of evidence and proof. Thus even in a case where the notice is returned with the endorsement that the premises has always been found locked or the addressee was not available at the time of postal delivery, it will be open to the complainant to prove at the trial by evidence that the endorsement is not correct and that the addressee, namely, the drawer of the cheque, with knowledge of the notice had deliberately avoided to receive notice." The important aspect to note in the above discussion as far as the present case is concerned is the insistence by the Court that there must be some endorsement on the postal cover of the noticee having left, or not being found or refusing service of notice. The facts in D.Vinod Shivappa were that the legal notice sent to the drawer of the dishonoured cheque by registered post was returned unserved with an endorsement "Party not in station, arrival not known". That was again not a case where nothing had been heard from the postal department after the notice was dispatched. It was in those circumstances that the Supreme Court held that Section 27 GCA could be invoked to presume service of notice. "23. We then turn to the case of C.C. Alavi Hazi. In para 18 of the said judgment , the facts are narrated. There the complainant issued a lawyer‟s notice which was returned with the endorsement that the accused was out of station. Therefore, that was again a case where the notice was returned with some endorsement or remark. It is plain from the above decisions that there has to be some feedback in the form of a postal endorsement that the notice was refused or not taken delivery of or that the noticee has left. Further, in such cases, it will be for the Court to draw an inference that service must be presumed. This is not an automatic conclusion to be drawn but an assessment to be made by the court keeping in view the the facts of the case." 34. Thus the legal position which emerges from the discussion herein above is that presumption of service of legal notice can be raised by the Court in cases where the envelope has been returned with endorsement "Party not in station, arrival not known", "addressee left" Addressee refused".
